anomaly_def.Name: Optimizer Statistics Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly: Row-count, histogram, and correlation metadata are stale, absent, or overly coarse, causing systematic cardinality misestimation and misleading the cost model.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer’s decision logic or plan-reuse mechanism selects a sub-optimal execution plan even when statistical inputs are acceptable, leading to inefficient access paths, join orders, or degrees of parallelism.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, threads, or other OS-managed objects, preventing the allocation of additional resources despite apparent database availability.

When all three anomalies coexist, the workload exhibits a volatile mix of wrong estimates, erratic plan flips, and hard OS-level allocation failures. Symptoms may include: 
• Extreme divergence between estimated and actual row counts followed by sudden switches between radically different plans.
• Queries that oscillate between sluggish full scans and explosive nested-loop iterations, creating bursts of temporary objects, file handles, or worker threads until OS limits are hit.
• Intermittent errors such as "cannot allocate shared memory" or "too many open files" appearing in tandem with frequent plan recompilations and statistics refresh attempts.
• Degradation that is hard to triage because poor plans inflate resource consumption, which in turn triggers kernel denials, causing further plan invalidations or forced serial execution.

Causal chain: Stale or incomplete statistics mislead the cost model, increasing the search space of viable plans. The plan-selection anomaly may then lock in an inefficient plan (e.g., parallel hash join with excessive workers or a nested loop with underestimated outer rows). The bloated plan drives higher memory, file-handle, and thread demands, quickly exhausting conservative OS quotas. Once these limits are reached, parallel worker launches, temporary-file creation, or I/O contexts fail, prompting the optimizer to recompile statements or fall back to even less efficient serial plans that run longer and generate more data modifications—further invalidating already stale statistics. This feedback loop intensifies contention, widens the gap between estimated and actual costs, and produces a cascading performance crisis that is more severe than any single anomaly would cause in isolation.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
